Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
 +3
Documented Origins: Aristotle was a citizen of Stagira in Macedonia. Theophrastus (originally named Tyrtamus) was a refugee from Eresos on the island of Lesbos. Ancient records even preserve the fact that Aristotle gave him the nickname "Theophrastus" (meaning "divine speaker") because of his distinct speaking style.
2. Empirical Divergences in Their Work
If "Aristotle" and "Theophrastus" were merely names pinned onto a single uniform mind, their observations of the natural world would not fundamentally clash. Empirically, however, they focused on different fields and arrived at opposing conclusions:
The Zoological vs. Botanical Split: Aristotle was a zoologist who focused deeply on marine life, animal dissection, and teleology (the idea that everything in nature has a human-centric or ultimate purpose). Theophrastus is the undisputed "Father of Botany". He spent his life classifying over 500 plant species in Enquiry into Plants, mapping plant physiology and ecosystems with a precision entirely absent from Aristotle’s surviving work.

 +3

While Aristotle claimed the natural world existed strictly for the sake of human beings, Theophrastus explicitly argued against this anthropocentric view, focusing instead on complex environmental relationships. He also vehemently disagreed with Aristotle regarding animal intelligence, arguing that animals share a deep sensory kinship with humans and should not be denied justice or moral consideration. 

Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
3. Historical External Testimony
The ancient world treated them as distinct, separate entities in real-time civic life:
Athenian Politics: In 307 BCE, an Athenian law briefly banned philosophers from running schools. Theophrastus was personally driven into exile by this decree and later returned in triumph when the law was repealed. Aristotle had faced a entirely separate wave of anti-Macedonian hostility decades prior, fleeing to Chalcis where he died.
Contemporary Accounts: Playwrights, political figures (like Demetrius of Phalerum), and competing philosophical schools (like the Epicureans and Stoics) explicitly wrote about, argued with, or supported Theophrastus as an independent intellectual leader, completely separate from the memory of his deceased master. 

The University of Chicago
 +4
In short, while their collaborative notes became physically intertwined over centuries of library survival, the empirical reality is that they were two separate human beings who left behind distinct legal footprints, distinct biographical lifespans, and fundamentally conflicting ideas.
